Q: How to limit accepted SSL/TLS versions when using Sim800 A:

For SIM800L the latest supported TSL is 1.0.
I couldn't find online firmware that support modern TSL encryption. cause of hardware version limitation.
You can use server/proxy the receives TSL1.0 and creates TSL1.2 or TSL1.3 request.

Q: I have a working docker-compose.yaml - what specifically will kompose convert NOT carry over into production-grade Kubernetes manifests? A:

Kubernetes just doesn't have several of the concepts you describe. It doesn't for example have multiple isolated networks (though the practical answer for almost all Compose files is to delete all of the manual networks: declarations); it doesn't have cross-service startup-order dependencies; you pretty much always need an image registry and can't build things in-cluster; you can't bind-mount content from a local system into the cluster.

The Kompose Conversion Matrix highlights a couple of the things you ask about. build: can work, if you already have an image registry. volumes: translate into PersistentVolumeClaims, which are right only for the case where you'd mount a named volume into a container and don't need the Docker feature that populates volumes from image content; they won't work for injecting local config files.

If you use the Compose configs: option (I have never personally seen or written this) then it at least translates into Kubernetes ConfigMaps, and similarly Compose secrets: can turn into Kubernetes Secrets (remember, not as secret as the name implies).

There are a couple of scaling and stability things that help. Kompose will never produce a PodDisruptionBudget (which prevents an administrator from taking a node offline if it's running the last copy of your Pod) or a HorizontalPodAutoscaler (which can create more copies of your Deployment under load). Ingress and Gateway objects to get external access to your application aren't supported. Some more controlled environments require NetworkPolicies for cross-service calls and Kompose doesn't support those.

IME Kompose hasn't done that great a job (though the feature matrix does look better than the last time I looked) and if you want Kubernetes support you'll be better off hand-writing it, or taking the kompose convert output and using it as the base for your own hand-maintained manifests or Helm charts.

Q: How to use a list in a pattern in re.match A:

You could make a regex which combines all the NrV (aka parts) and then scan the full file list.

Also, your question has "a+ just means the capital version of that letter" but your expected result is ['_a-.wav', '_a+-.wav] rather than ['_a-.wav', '_A-.wav]. I'm going to assume you want 'a' and 'a+' instead of 'a' and 'A'.

(I'm going to use the same variable names as in furas' answer.)

#import os
import re

parts = ["a", "a+"]
all_parts_regex = re.compile("|".join(fr"_{re.escape(part)}-" for part in parts))
# print(all_parts_regex.pattern)  # for FYI/debug
# printed pattern is: _a-|_a\+-

filenames = ["_a-.wav", "_b-.wav", "a.wav", "_a+-.wav"]
# filenames = os.listdir(...)

# use re.match since you want to match at the start of the filename
filtered_filenames = [filename for filename in filenames if all_parts_regex.match(filename)]
print(f"{filtered_filenames=}")
print("result:", filtered_filenames == ["_a-.wav", "_a+-.wav"])

If you really are doing "a+ just means the capital version of that letter" then you can simplify the parts list: Put only the lowercase letter and (1) then add the uppercases before constructing the regex. Or (2) make the regex match case-insensitive with the re.IGNORECASE flag.

(1.) Put the lowercase and then add the uppercases programmatically

# only put the lowercase letters here
parts = ["a", "x", "y", "z"]
# add the uppercases
parts.extend([letter.upper() for letter in parts])

# re.escape not needed here; even the 'r' raw string prefix is not needed
all_parts_regex = re.compile("|".join(fr"_{letter}-" for letter in parts))
# print(all_parts_regex.pattern)  # for FYI/debug
# printed pattern is: _a-|_x-|_y-|_z-|_A-|_X-|_Y-|_Z-

# what the actual filenames would have been, note the last `_A-.wav`
filenames = ["_a-.wav", "_b-.wav", "a.wav", "_A-.wav"]
# filenames = os.listdir(...)

filtered_filenames = [filename for filename in filenames if all_parts_regex.match(filename)]
print(f"{filtered_filenames=}")
print("result:", filtered_filenames == ["_a-.wav", "_A-.wav"])

(2.) Using case-insensitive matching

parts = ["a", "x", "y", "z"]
all_parts_regex = re.compile("|".join(fr"_{letter}-" for letter in parts), re.IGNORECASE)
filenames = ["_a-.wav", "_b-.wav", "a.wav", "_A-.wav"]
filtered_filenames = [filename for filename in filenames if all_parts_regex.match(filename)]

Q: Explain the difference and similarity between two code blocks A:

Here is a breakdown of the similarities and differences between a repeat (10) block and a forever block (commonly found in block-based programming environments like Scratch):

Similarities:

  1. Control Flow Structures: Both are loop control structures used to repeat a sequence of actions or code blocks sequentially.

  2. Execution Logic: Both execute the nested blocks inside them line-by-line until the loop's condition/limit is reached or interrupted.

  3. Automation: Both reduce code duplication by preventing developers or users from writing the same set of instructions manually over and over again.

Differences:

  1. Termination / Duration:

    • repeat (10): This is a finite (bounded) loop. It runs the enclosed code a fixed, predetermined number of times (in this case, exactly 10 times) and then automatically terminates, moving on to the next code block.

    • forever: This is an infinite (unbounded) loop. It continues running the enclosed code indefinitely without stopping, unless an explicit break condition, stop event, or external interruption occurs.

  2. Use Cases:

    • repeat (10) is ideal when you know the exact number of iterations needed (e.g., moving a character forward 10 steps, counting down, or spawning a specific number of items).

    • forever is used for continuous background tasks that need to run as long as the program or game is active (e.g., checking for user input, continuous movement animation, or game loop updates).
